t: Maximum Number of Removable Characters — Binary Search the Removal Count
o: p is already a subsequence of s. We must remove characters at removable[0], removable[1], ... in that exact order, and find the largest k such that after removing the first k indices, p is still a subsequence of s. Example 1: s = "abcacb", p = "ab", removable = [3,1,0] — deleting indices 3 and 1 leaves "accb", where "ab" can still be matched; deleting index 0 as well leaves "ccb", which lost its 'a', so the answer is 2. Example 3 shows k = 0 is possible when even the first removal breaks p. The structural key is monotonicity: once p stops being a subsequence it stays broken under further removals, so feasibility is a step function of k — ideal for binary search. With |s| up to 10^5, each feasibility check must be a single linear two-pointer pass.
k: Feasibility is monotone in k — if p survives the first k removals it survives every smaller count — so the answer is a threshold binary search can locate.
A feasibility check marks the first k removable indices, then greedily matches p through the surviving letters of s with one linear scan.
Total cost O((n + m) log k) comfortably handles n up to 10^5; an incremental scan from k = 0 upward also works but degenerates to quadratic.

a.n: Approach 1: Incremental Removal with Early Exit
a.i: Apply removals one at a time and re-test p after each. The first failing removal index is exactly the answer because every earlier state was still feasible. Simple and easy to defend in an interview, though repeated rescans make it quadratic when the answer is large.
s: Keep a boolean removed array over s.
For k = 0, 1, 2, ...: mark removable[k], then run a two-pointer subsequence test of p against unmarked characters of s.
On the first failure return the current k.
If all removals succeed, return removable.length.
a.t: O(R x (n + m)) with R = removable.length — up to R full rescans of s.

a.i: Monotonicity licenses a direct binary search over the answer. check(k) marks removable[0..k-1] and verifies p greedily; the predicate holds on a prefix of values 0..R, so an upper-bias binary search converges to the boundary in log R checks. This trades approach 1's linear ramp for logarithmic passes.
s: Define check(k): reset marks, mark removable[0..k-1], match p through unmarked characters of s, return whether all of p was consumed.
Binary search with lo = 0, hi = R using upper mid mid = (lo + hi + 1) / 2.
If check(mid) holds set lo = mid, else set hi = mid - 1.
a.t: O((n + m) log R) — about log R feasibility scans, each linear in s plus p.
a.sp: O(n) — the marks array (or a hash set of marked indices).

w: Say the word monotone out loud — it is what licenses binary search here, as in most 'maximize k such that...' problems. Pitfalls: forgetting that removable order is mandatory (you cannot cherry-pick indices), off-by-one errors in the upper-mid binary search pattern (mid = (lo+hi+1)/2 with lo = mid), and rebuilding mark structures inefficiently when resetting a reused array suffices. Edge cases: answer 0 (Example 3) and answer removable.length. Follow-up: many independent queries of this shape invite parallel binary search across queries.
